cases.answerText:
**Yes.** Under the 2022 NYC Building Code, glazing in any fixed or operable panel of a swinging door is considered a hazardous location and must be safety glazing, unless an exception applies. One exception covers an opening too small for a 3-inch-diameter sphere to pass through; the other listed exceptions are decorative glazing, curved glazing in revolving doors, and commercial refrigerated-cabinet glazed doors. (BC §§ 2406.4, 2406.4.1)

This rule is about glazing *in* the swinging door. Glazing adjacent to a door is addressed separately and has its own conditions and exceptions; it is not the rule for glazing in the door itself. (BC § 2406.4.2)

cases.label: correct_useful
cases.note: Core rule and exception scope match paired source key.
cases.answerText: **Yes, if the glazing is in an individual fixed or operable panel adjacent to the door.** Under the 2022 NYC Building Code, such glazing is considered a hazardous location when its nearest vertical edge is within a 24-inch arc of either vertical edge of the closed door and its bottom exposed edge is less than 60 inches above the walking surface. At 40 inches, the stated glazing meets that height condition; on the individual-panel condition above and with no exception, it is hazardous. (BC § 2406.4.2)

cases.answerText: Yes. Under the 2022 NYC Building Code, when glazing in a shower enclosure meets the hazardous-location condition—its bottom exposed edge is less than 60 inches above a standing or walking surface—the rule expressly applies to “single glazing and all panes in multiple glazing.” The stated exception concerns glazing more than 60 inches horizontally, in a straight line, from the water’s edge of a bathtub, hot tub, spa, whirlpool, or swimming pool; it does not list a shower. (BC § 2406.4.5)

cases.label: correct_useful
cases.note: Core answer matches paired source-reviewed rule.
cases.answerText:
**Yes, conditionally:** BC 2406.4.7 treats glazing at the bottom stairway landing as hazardous when it is **less than 60 inches above the landing** and within a **60-inch horizontal arc of less than 180 degrees from the bottom-tread nosing**. At 40 inches, the height condition is met; the stated arc condition must also be met. The exception applies if the glazing is protected by a guard complying with Sections 1015 and 1607.8 and the glass plane is more than 18 inches from the guard. (BC § 2406.4.7)

The separate stairway-and-ramp rule also treats glazing with its bottom exposed edge less than 60 inches above the adjacent walking surface as hazardous, subject to its stated guard and 36-inch-horizontal-distance exceptions. (BC § 2406.4.6)

cases.answerText: The ordinary minimum is **8 feet (2438.4 mm) in any plan dimension** for a habitable space other than a kitchen (BC § 1208.1). This is the baseline when no exception applies. The separate minimum net floor area is 80 square feet (7.4 m²) (BC § 1208.3.1).

cases.answerText: **No.** Under the 2022 NYC Plumbing Code, a shower compartment must be at least **900 square inches** in interior cross-sectional area **and** at least **30 inches** in its least dimension, measured from the finished interior dimension. Thus 950 square inches satisfies the area minimum, but a 28-inch least dimension does not satisfy the separate 30-inch minimum (PC § 417.4).

cases.answerText: Yes. Under the 2022 NYC Plumbing Code, lavatories in public toilet facilities provided for customers, patrons, or visitors must deliver tempered water. Normally it must pass through an approved temperature-limiting device conforming to ASSE 1070; where point-of-use heaters are installed, the outlet temperature must instead be regulated to provide tempered water (PC § 416.5).

cases.answerText: Yes. Under the 2022 NYC Plumbing Code, rooms containing automatic clothes washers in a central washing facility of a multiple-family dwelling must have floor drains positioned to readily drain the entire floor area. Each drain must have an outlet at least 3 inches in diameter and a lint strainer (PC § 412.4). The general floor-drain provisions also require removable strainers and cleanable drains with access (PC § 412.2).

cases.answerText: No. Under the 2022 NYC Plumbing Code, drainage piping cannot decrease in size in the direction of flow, so an ordinary 4-inch-to-3-inch downstream reduction is not permitted. The stated exception is a 4-inch-by-3-inch water-closet connection, which is not considered a reduction in size (PC § 704.2).

cases.answerText: No. Under the 2022 NYC Plumbing Code, Table 706.3 shows a dash (–) for a sanitary tee in the horizontal-to-horizontal column, so it is not permitted for that change in direction. Section 706.3 also requires changes in direction to use fittings installed in accordance with the table (PC § 706.3).

cases.answerText:
For a lot 18 feet wide, the 2022 NYC Mechanical Code’s special rule is that a ventilation-air intake opening must be located at the centerline between the lot lines—not simply 10 feet from each lot line. The ordinary rule is at least 10 feet from lot lines or buildings on the same lot; if the opening fronts on a street or public way, measure the distance to that way’s centerline. (MC § 401.4)

This answers the lot-line location rule; other location requirements in § 401.4 may also apply depending on the intake and site conditions.

cases.answerText: No. For an intake opening serving a residential occupancy, the 2022 NYC Mechanical Code requires the screen openings to be at least 1/4 inch and no more than 1/2 inch; 3/4 inch exceeds that maximum (MC § 401.5). The separate Fuel Gas Code screen rule specifies 1/4-inch openings for required outdoor air inlets serving residential portions of a building (FGC § 618.5).

cases.answerText:
**No.** Under the 2022 NYC Mechanical Code, outdoor air required by Section 403.3.1.1 may not be recirculated (MC § 403.2.1). Air supplied in excess of that required amount may generally be recirculated, subject to the stated restrictions: ventilation air may not be recirculated between dwelling units or to dissimilar occupancies; pool and associated-deck air is restricted; and certain spaces identified by Table 403.3.1.1 Notes b or g have additional recirculation and exhaust restrictions. Transfer air may serve required exhaust as permitted, but the required outdoor airflow must still be introduced directly into the relevant spaces, into the spaces from which air is transferred, or both (MC § 403.2.2).

The supplied text does not include the complete table or its notes, so the note-specific restrictions and required airflow for a particular space cannot be determined from this packet.

cases.answerText: **Yes, in principle.** The 2022 NYC Mechanical Code permits air transferred from occupiable spaces to serve as makeup air for required exhaust systems in baths, unless the applicable Table 403.3.1.1 provision prohibits it. The transfer and exhaust amounts must provide the rates specified by that section, and required outdoor airflow must be introduced into the bathroom, the spaces supplying the transfer air, or both (MC § 403.2.2). The supplied table text is incomplete, so whether its exception applies to a particular bathroom classification cannot be determined here.

cases.answerText: Intermittent mechanical ventilation in an enclosed parking garage is controlled by **both carbon monoxide (CO) and nitrogen dioxide (NO₂) detectors**, used together. The system must operate automatically at **CO 25 ppm or NO₂ 500 ppb**, and the detectors must be installed according to their manufacturers’ instructions (2022 NYC MC § 404.1).

The separate dryer-closet provision allows a closet opening of at least 100 square inches instead of makeup air provided by other approved means; the supplied text does not state that this alternative removes the requirement triggered by exhausting more than 200 cfm.

**The supplied text does not establish a blanket smoking prohibition** in an ordinary Group M occupancy. It prohibits smoking where a “No Smoking” sign is posted for fire-safety purposes; separately, it addresses non-tobacco smoking at lawfully operating hookah establishments. The mechanical-code provision assumes no smoking for baseline ventilation and requires additional ventilation if smoking is anticipated outside a non-tobacco hookah establishment—but that ventilation rule does not itself authorize smoking or prohibit it. (FC § 310.5; MC § 403.3.1.1)

A definitive answer about whether another applicable Fire Code provision prohibits smoking in the stated occupancy cannot be resolved from this packet: FC § 310 is supplied only in part, and its listed reference to FC § 283 is missing.

cases.label: correct_useful
cases.note: Ownership and recorded binding restrictions correctly identified; maintains district applicability boundary.
cases.answerText:
**No.** Required off-site parking spaces cannot rely solely on a revocable informal arrangement: the applicable Zoning Resolution provision requires deed restrictions filed in an office of record, binding the owner and successors to keep the required spaces available throughout the life of the use. It also requires the spaces to be in the same ownership as the use, either through single-fee ownership or an alternative ownership arrangement described in ZR § 12-10. (ZR §§ 25-55, 36-45, 44-34)

Which off-site provision applies depends on the district and the basis for providing the spaces. The supplied ZR § 44-32, for example, permits certain off-site spaces in M1–M3 districts subject to location limits; that does not establish which provision governs a particular site. The supplied § 12-10 excerpt does not include the referenced definition of alternative ownership arrangements, so its full scope cannot be determined here.
